paras: The threatened lynching of Boge Jackson and Henry Hill took place at Hamburg, Arkansas, on October 22, 1881, when a crowd of several thousand that had gathered to see the two Black men hanged learned that the governor had reprieved them. Many in the crowd wanted to lynch the prisoners, and one report said they were held back only with great effort, but no attack is reported. Hill's sentence was later commuted to life imprisonment, and Jackson was legally hanged at Hamburg on November 18.

According to a Little Rock dispatch in the Memphis Appeal, Jackson had quarreled with a colored neighbor, Reuben Jordan, over a division fence that stood on Jordan's land. Jordan was shot on the night of February 15, 1881, while walking home from the village, and Jackson was arrested and charged with the killing, with Hill named as an accessory. Both men were sentenced to be hanged on October 22 at Hamburg, which the Appeal described as the seat of Ashley County.

All preparations for the execution had been made, and a crowd of several thousand persons, "mostly colored," had gathered to watch it. The Wichita City Eagle put the crowd at some three thousand and said many had traveled a hundred miles to see "the sport." Governor Churchill granted a reprieve, which the Kansas paper said arrived by messenger at the last moment.

The wire brief said the crowd's "disgust was so great at being cheated out of the ghastly spectacle, that many wanted to lynch the prisoners." The Wichita account went further, saying that only "the most strenuous exertions" kept the people from lynching "the poor fellow," though it did not say who restrained them. Neither report describes any seizure, injury or attack on the prisoners.

The Memphis Appeal reported that Jackson was respited until November 18 and that Hill's sentence was commuted to life imprisonment. Jackson was hanged at Hamburg on November 18 before several thousand spectators, "white and black." Dispatches from Little Rock described him as a native of Mississippi who had served a prison term there for manslaughter and called him "a noted desperado."

The Wichita City Eagle carried the first known report on November 10, a short item that named no one and mocked the crowd's appetite for a hanging. Two days later an identical brief, calling the prisoners "two colored murderers," ran unheadlined in the news roundups of the Huntsville Gazette, the Milan Exchange, the Southern Standard and the American Citizen. That brief placed Hamburg in "Jackson County," an error the later Little Rock dispatches corrected to Ashley County.

Coverage of Jackson's legal execution on November 18 was wider and said nothing of the earlier lynching threat. The Evening Star and the National Republican printed the Little Rock dispatch, the latter under the heading "Necks Elongated," and the Memphis Appeal headlined its long account "A Fitting Sequel to a Life of Iniquity." Weekly roundups in Wisconsin, Kansas, Virginia and Missouri reduced the execution to a line or two over the following week.

The wire brief named two reprieved prisoners, while the Wichita item spoke of a single "doomed man." The wire also said the governor reprieved both men, whereas the Memphis Appeal reported a respite for Jackson and a commutation for Hill, without saying when the commutation was granted.

reader.title: Threatened lynching of Boge Jackson and Henry Hill
bases: A crowd gathered for a legal hanging at Hamburg turned on the reprieved prisoners, and many in it wanted to lynch them or had to be restrained from doing so, though no attack is reported (A1, A2).

No one was killed: the threat came from 'many' in a crowd of thousands angry that the convicted men would not hang (A1, A2), and Jackson was later executed legally while Hill's sentence was commuted (A9).

Two differently worded reports, a wire brief (A2, reprinted A3-A5) and a Kansas item (A1), agree that a crowd of thousands at Hamburg was cheated of a hanging by a reprieve and wanted to lynch the condemned; the Memphis Appeal confirms the Oct. 22 sentence and the respite (A9).

accounts.label: Wire brief
accounts.gist: Churchill reprieved two colored murderers, Jackson and Hill, due to hang Oct. 22; several thousand people, mostly colored, had gathered, and many were so disgusted at missing the spectacle that they wanted to lynch the prisoners.

accounts.label: Kansas item
accounts.gist: Some 3,000 people, many from a hundred miles away, came to Hamburg to see a hanging; a last-moment reprieve for 'the doomed man' so disappointed them that only strenuous exertions kept them from lynching him.

accounts.label: Little Rock dispatch
accounts.gist: Jackson and Hill were first sentenced to hang Oct. 22; Jackson was respited to Nov. 18 and hanged, while Hill's sentence was commuted to life; it says nothing of a lynching threat.

framing.detail: An unheadlined item in 'Personal and General' and 'Miscellaneous' roundups, speaking of 'colored murderers' and the crowd's 'disgust' at being 'cheated out of the ghastly spectacle'.
The Wichita item calls the hanging 'the sport' and the prisoner 'the poor fellow', mocking the crowd's appetite.
The Memphis Appeal headlined the later legal execution 'A Fitting Sequel to a Life of Iniquity' and did not mention the lynching threat.

conflicts.note: The Little Rock dispatches (A6, A7) and the Memphis Appeal, which calls Hamburg the Ashley County seat (A9), are the better evidence; the wire brief's 'Jackson County' likely confuses the prisoner's name with the county.
A1 names no one; A2 and A9 both name two condemned men.

conflicts.note: A1 implies an effort to seize the prisoner that had to be checked; A2 reports only the wish. Neither says who restrained the crowd.
